aximar.title: Messages from Maxima
aximar.description: How Aximar explains Maxima's errors, questions and notes, and how to answer a question.

cells.source:
# Messages from Maxima

Besides results, Maxima tells you things in three ways: **errors** when a cell can't finish, **questions** when it needs to know more, and **notes** about what it did along the way. Aximar explains each one in plain language, and in your language when Aximar has a translation (Settings, Language).

Several cells here fail on purpose, so run them one at a time with Shift+Enter rather than Run All, which stops at the first error.

## Errors

When a cell fails, Aximar shows what went wrong and how to fix it. The error exactly as Maxima printed it is one click away, under **Show raw error**.
Some explanations name the parts of your input involved. Here `f` takes one argument but gets two:
Syntax errors say which kind they are, such as a bracket that was never closed:
sin(x;
Errors from the Lisp system Maxima runs on keep their whole message, and the common ones are explained. This recursion never stops:

## Questions

Sometimes Maxima needs a fact before it can go on, such as the sign of a symbol. In a terminal it would ask and wait for an answer. A notebook can't answer, so Aximar stops the cell, shows the question, and suggests a line that answers it.
integrate(exp(-a*x), x, 0, inf);
Add the suggested line before the computation and run the cell again. Because the answer is in the notebook, it runs the same way every time:

assume(a > 0)$
integrate(exp(-a*x), x, 0, inf);
Other questions ask whether two things are equal, or whether a symbol is an integer. Each gets its own suggestion:
integrate(x^n, x);

assume(notequal(n, -1))$
integrate(x^n, x);
A question isn't an ordinary error: `errcatch` doesn't hide it, so a question inside your own error handling still reaches you.
errcatch(integrate(exp(-b*x), x, 0, inf));
`forget` takes an assumption back:
forget(a > 0, notequal(n, -1))$

## Notes

Maxima prints notes about what it did, such as turning decimals into fractions. Aximar shows each note as one line in plain language, in place of Maxima's text. **Show Maxima's text** brings the original back.
`solve` warns when it uses inverse trigonometric functions, because some solutions get lost:
solve(sin(x) = 1/2, x);
And `integrate` says when a result is a principal value, because the integral diverges inside the range:
integrate(1/x, x, -1, 1);
Text you print yourself is never mistaken for a note:
print("rat: this is my own text")$

## In your language

With a language other than English chosen in Settings, explanations and notes show in that language. When Maxima has its own translation of an error message, it appears under Aximar's explanation, with **Show original** for Maxima's English. Results, printed text and code always stay as Maxima gives them.
